title: India's Central Bank Is Offering NRIs a Rare Deal — Dollar Deposits at Up to 7.5% With Zero Currency Risk
excerpt: The RBI has removed interest rate ceilings on FCNR deposits and is absorbing the full hedging cost. Banks have responded with rate hikes of up to 450 basis points. The window closes September 30.
body:
If you're an NRI with dollars sitting in a savings account earning 4 percent, the Reserve Bank of India just made you an offer that probably won't last.

In a sweeping set of measures announced on June 5 and expanded on June 17, the RBI has effectively created a time-limited window for overseas Indians to park their dollars in Indian banks at interest rates of **6 to 7.5 percent** — with the central bank itself absorbing the currency risk that has traditionally eaten into NRI deposit returns.

The window closes September 30, 2026. And Indian banks are racing to capture the inflows before it does.

## How the Deal Works

The mechanics are straightforward, though the backstory explains why this is unusual.

Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposits have always let NRIs deposit dollars, euros, or pounds in Indian banks for fixed terms of one to five years. The catch was the interest rate: because banks had to hedge against rupee depreciation — buying insurance, essentially, that the rupee wouldn't weaken before the deposit matured — the hedging cost ate into what they could offer. With annualized hedging costs of roughly 2.9 to 3 percent, an NRI depositor was typically looking at returns of just 3 to 3.5 percent.

The RBI's new scheme changes the equation entirely. The central bank has announced it will **bear the full hedging cost** on fresh FCNR deposits of 3 to 5 years. On June 17, it went further, **temporarily removing the interest rate ceiling** on these deposits entirely.

The result: banks can now offer rates that reflect India's domestic deposit rates without the hedging haircut.

## What Banks Are Offering

The response has been swift and aggressive:

- **SBI**: 5.25% to 6% on 3-5 year USD deposits (up to 300 bps higher)
- **HDFC Bank**: 6% on 3-5 year deposits (up 235-265 bps)
- **ICICI Bank**: 6% on select tenures (up 310 bps)
- **Axis Bank**: 6% on 3-5 year deposits (up 305 bps)
- **AU Small Finance Bank**: Up to 7.1% on 3-year deposits
- **Yes Bank**: 7% to 7.1% on 3-5 year deposits

Outlook Money reports that some smaller banks are offering rates approaching **7.5 percent** after the RBI removed the interest rate ceiling.

For context, a 5-year US Treasury currently yields about 3.9 percent. A 5-year CD from a top US bank offers roughly 4 to 4.3 percent. The FCNR rates represent a meaningful premium — and unlike Indian domestic deposits, the returns are in dollars, tax-free in India, and fully repatriable.

## Why the RBI Is Doing This

The scheme is not philanthropy. The rupee has been Asia's second-worst-performing currency in 2026, falling roughly 6 percent and hitting record lows in May. India's foreign exchange reserves need bolstering, and the RBI is leaning on the diaspora — the 37-million-strong global Indian community — to provide a lifeline.

It's not the first time. In 2013, facing a similar rupee crisis, the RBI launched a nearly identical FCNR-B scheme that attracted $26 billion in deposits and another $8 billion in external commercial borrowings, helping stabilize the currency.

This time, analysts expect the haul to be larger. **Nomura estimates potential inflows of $55 billion**. **Axis Bank sees scope for up to $100 billion.** The more liberal terms — no interest rate ceiling, full hedging cost absorption, exemptions from statutory liquidity and cash reserve ratios — make the 2026 scheme more attractive than its predecessor.

Jefferies noted that HDFC Bank was the largest mobilizer under the 2013 scheme, pulling in $3.4 billion (7 percent of its total deposits at the time), and is likely to be a key beneficiary again.

## What NRIs Should Know

**The basics**: FCNR deposits are denominated in foreign currency — your dollars go in and come out as dollars. Interest is paid in the same currency. The principal and interest are fully repatriable and **tax-free in India**.

**The lock-in**: Deposits booked under the special scheme (3-5 year tenures) carry a **one-year lock-in period**. No interest is paid on premature withdrawal before one year, and early exit after one year may carry penalties.

**The risk profile**: Currency risk is zero — the RBI is bearing it. Credit risk is minimal — these are deposits at regulated Indian banks, and FCNR deposits up to ₹5 lakh (roughly $6,000) are covered by deposit insurance. For larger amounts, the risk is essentially the solvency of India's banking system, which is well-capitalized by global standards.

**The leverage question**: In 2013, some depositors leveraged their personal funds 10-20x by borrowing dollars abroad and depositing them in India, pocketing the spread. The RBI has signaled it may allow similar arrangements through overseas branches and GIFT City, but clarity is still pending. For most retail NRIs, the straightforward play is using existing savings.

**Tax implications abroad**: While FCNR interest is tax-free in India, NRIs in the US, UK, or Canada will still owe taxes on the interest income in their country of residence. Consult a cross-border tax advisor.

## The Clock Is Ticking

The scheme's terms expire September 30, 2026. After that, the interest rate ceiling returns, the RBI stops absorbing hedging costs, and FCNR rates will likely fall back to the 3-3.5 percent range.

For NRIs with idle dollar savings — or those weighing where to park short-term liquidity — the next three months represent a rare window where India's banking system is offering a genuine premium for their capital, with the central bank underwriting the currency risk.

The RBI is, in effect, paying a premium for the diaspora's trust. Whether that trust — and those dollars — show up in time to help the rupee will be one of the more consequential financial stories of the year.
